criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community domestic drinking and bathing water service access alongside agricultural and other uses within the Kirindi Oya irrigation system, specifically analysing piped water supply standposts operated by the National Water Supply and Drainage Board (NWS&DB), wells, and dry-season domestic canal water releases.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the paper examines water rights, institutional mandates, and participatory governance structures (Farmers' Organizations, Standpipe Committees, Project Management Committee). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines formal regulatory, tariff, enforcement, eligibility, and informal accommodation rules governing household domestic water access: NWS&DB rules restricting standpipe water strictly to drinking use (and prohibiting garden watering from piped supplies or canals), Rs 11/month household user charges, collective standpipe committee liability with service disconnection and a Rs 250 reconnection fee for rule violations, informal standpost-level discretion/accommodation for non-drinking uses and pilgrims, reservoir allocation priority rules for domestic supply during drought, and formal membership rules restricting Farmers' Organizations to irrigated land cultivators while excluding NWS&DB and domestic water user groups from the Project Management Committee.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods / socio-legal empirical fieldwork conducted by IWMI, IFPRI, and ICRW, comprising a stratified household survey (78 households in the old area and 78 in the new area, n = 156), water quality testing, direct observations at standpipes and tanks, approximately 10 focus group discussions, and key informant interviews with NWS&DB and Irrigation Department officials and Standpipe Committee and Farmer Organization representatives. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible regardless of whether they report a quantitative effect estimate.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports empirical outcomes relevant to domestic water access, source reliance, permitted uses, availability during scarcity, and service continuity/reliability, including low standpipe supply reliability (water supplied only a few hours per day at varying hours), reliance on piped water in the new area versus wells in the old area, dry-season 14-day domestic water issues, emergency protection vs. subordination of domestic allocations during scarcity (1992, 1995, 1997), and de facto household access to standpipe water for bathing, laundry, and micro-enterprises where alternative sources are lacking.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and sample (87,750 residents in old and new settlement areas of Kirindi Oya, Sri Lanka; stratified survey of 156 households, ~10 focus groups, standpipe/tank observations, and key informant interviews), legal/institutional exposures (formal vs. informal water rights, NWS&DB standpost tariff/use/disconnection rules, and sectoral membership/representation rules), access/reliability outcomes, and an empirical case-study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: A certain amount of Lunugamwehera reservoir water is set aside for domestic water supply. Most of this is a ﬁxed allocation to the NWS&DB to operate the piped water supply system that serves especially the new area.

These standpipe committees are informal, i.e., no authority is vested in them, although they are responsible for collecting user charges of Rs 11 per month from the households who make use of the standposts.

The formal rules are speciﬁed by the NWS&DB, with little user involvement. Informally, however, each group decides what uses will be tolerated or even considered legitimate, so there are some de facto management rights.

Further direct observations at standpipes and tanks were done and about 10 focus group discussions with, among others, women cultivators and curd pot makers. These methods were used to identify different categories of uses and users. Key informant interviews were executed to derive the implications for management of the irrigation system.
Reliability of water supply through standpipes is quite low. Water is supplied for only a few hours a day and these hours can vary every day.

raw_response.exposure: Formal and informal water rights and regulatory rules governing multiple uses and domestic piped water supply, including NWS&DB standpost rules (drinking-only use restriction, prohibition on garden watering, Rs 11/month household user charge, collective standpipe committee liability with service disconnection and Rs 250 reconnection fee), local standpost accommodation/discretion norms, seasonal/drought domestic water allocation priority rules, and user-organization membership and Project Management Committee representation rules (restricting Farmers' Organization membership to irrigated land cultivators and omitting NWS&DB and Standpipe Committees).
raw_response.outcome: Household and community domestic water access and source reliance (piped standposts vs. wells and dry-season 14-day canal releases), standpipe supply continuity/reliability (hours of supply per day and daily variability), de facto tolerated water uses at standposts under threat of disconnection, and representation/prioritization of domestic water needs during water scarcity.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households and water user groups in the old Ellegala and new settlement areas of the Kirindi Oya irrigation system, southeastern Sri Lanka (~87,750 inhabitants; 15 to 20 households per NWS&DB standpost); primary fieldwork sampled 156 households in a stratified survey (78 in the old area and 78 in the new area), alongside ~10 focus group discussions, direct observations at standpipes and tanks, and key informant interviews with government officials and user-group representatives.
raw_response.rationale: Although framed around multiple uses of an irrigation common-pool system, this empirical socio-legal case study is directly relevant to household and community domestic water service access (thus not excluded under Exclusion Criterion 7). Based on a stratified survey of 156 households, direct standpipe observations, focus groups, and key informant interviews in Kirindi Oya, Sri Lanka, the paper examines rule-type mechanisms directly governing domestic piped water access—including NWS&DB permitted-use rules, monthly user charges (Rs 11), collective enforcement via disconnection and a Rs 250 reconnection fee, informal community accommodation at standposts, drought allocation priority rules, and institutional membership rules excluding non-irrigators, women, and domestic water agencies from allocation bodies—and reports qualitative empirical findings on source reliance, de facto access, and low standpipe supply reliability. Confidence is medium because domestic water supply is analysed as one component within a broader multi-use irrigation system study and outcomes are reported qualitatively rather than quantitatively, which remains fully eligible for the systematic review mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods / qualitative socio-legal empirical case study (stratified household survey, direct observations, focus group discussions, water quality measurements, and key informant interviews)
